issues: The content is correct. Recital 66 says: 'Where it is technically possible and effective, in accordance with the relevant provisions of Directive 95/46/EC, the user's consent to processing may be expressed by using the appropriate settings of a browser or other application.' Article 2(5), which replaces Article 5(3) of Directive 2002/58/EC, requires consent 'having been provided with clear and comprehensive information', and exempts storage or access that is strictly necessary. The Directive's recitals and Article 2 never use the words 'banner' or 'pop-up'.

Nuance, not an error: the last sentence ('Banners were how sites chose to implement it') leaves out that national regulators' guidance, and after 2018 the GDPR consent standard, pushed sites toward banners. It is still true that the Directive does not require them.

issues: legalForce puts in quotation marks a phrase the spec does not contain: 'no technical mechanism for making sure sites act according to their policies'. The spec reads: 'it does not provide a technical mechanism for making sure sites act according to their policies'. The record's paraphrase 'relies on laws and self-regulatory programmes' also has a verbatim source line: 'P3P is complementary to laws and self-regulatory programs that can provide enforcement mechanisms.'

The fate field says 'Little deployment beyond Internet Explorer's cookie filter'. That is wrong for this record: IE's cookie filter did not use full XML policies. It acted on compact policies, a separate signal with its own record. In the W3C's words, IE used 'the presence of a compact P3P policy as a broad gate'.

whatItSays says the policy is 'published at a well-known location'. The spec puts a policy reference file, not the policy itself, at the well-known path /w3c/p3p.xml, and makes that optional ('MAY'). Sites can instead point to it with a P3P HTTP header or a link tag.

Everything else checks out on the W3C pages. Recommendation 16 April 2002, 'obsoleted 30 August 2018'. 'fewer than 6% of the 10,000 most frequently visited websites support P3P' (2018, BuiltWith). 'no enforcement action followed'. Cranor (2012): 'no regulators have announced that they are investigating any website for a deceptive P3P policy'.

fieldFixes.whatItSays: The website's own data practices, in a fixed XML vocabulary: what it collects, for what purposes, for which recipients, how long it keeps data, whether people can access it and how disputes are resolved. A policy reference file tells user agents which policy covers which pages. A site may place that file at the well-known path /w3c/p3p.xml, or point to it with a P3P HTTP header or a link tag. The person's user agent fetches the policy and compares it with preferences the person has set. The person cannot send terms back.
fieldFixes.legalForce: None in itself. The specification says P3P 'does not provide a technical mechanism for making sure sites act according to their policies' and is 'complementary to laws and self-regulatory programs that can provide enforcement mechanisms'. No regulator is known to have acted against a deceptive P3P policy (Cranor, 2012; W3C, 2018).
fieldFixes.fate: Only limited deployment. Its main use, Internet Explorer's cookie filter, acted on the short compact policies rather than on full XML policies. Fewer than 6% of the 10,000 most-visited sites supported P3P in 2018, when the W3C declared it obsolete.

issues: whatItSays says IE's default Medium setting used compact policies 'to decide whether to accept, downgrade or block third-party cookies'. That misstates the rule. At Medium, third-party cookies were accepted or rejected: they were rejected if they had no compact policy or an unsatisfactory one. Downgrading to session cookies applied to unsatisfactory first-party cookies. CMU's report: 'Under the medium setting, unsatisfactory ﬁrst-party cookies are converted into session cookies and unsatisfactory third-party cookies are rejected. In addition, third-party cookies not accompanied by CPs are rejected.' Downgrading third-party cookies was only an optional custom template in the IEInternals post.

legalForce paraphrases the IEInternals footnote as the browser having 'no technical means' to 'verify' the claims. The source says 'enforce'. The same footnote also says 'a government or individual would have grounds to file a lawsuit' over a false policy, and Cranor (2012) argued the FTC or state attorneys general 'could go after' deceptive P3P policies. A bare 'None.' therefore overstates the case: the signal had no force of its own, but a false one was potentially actionable, and nobody acted on it.

The fate field has two problems. 'Google's and Facebook's non-policies were exposed in February 2012' overstates novelty: The Register's own report says the tactic had been 'pointed out by El Reg last year and in academic papers in 2010', and CMU's 2010 table already listed facebook.com's invalid 'DSP LAW' policy. And 'when no current browser acted on P3P' drops the attribution: the W3C wrote 'No current (2018) user agents are known to…'.

None of the record's sources supported the header text 'This is not a P3P policy!' or the Google/Facebook claim, so The Register and Cubrilovic are added. The numbers 11,176 of 33,139 and 98% are verbatim in the cited CMU abstract ('We collected CPs from 33,139 websites and detected errors in 11,176 of them'; '98% of invalid CPs resulted in cookies remaining unblocked by IE under it’s default cookie settings.'), both FOUND. 'three- and four-letter tokens' matches CMU's 'three-character and four-character tokens'.
Not verified here: the start year 2001 (IE6 shipped in August 2001). The sources say only 'used by IE 6, 7, and 8'.

fieldFixes.whatItSays: A string of three- and four-letter tokens summarising the site's cookie-related practices (purpose, recipients, retention, data categories), sent in the P3P HTTP response header that sets the cookie. Under Internet Explorer's default 'Medium' setting, a third-party cookie was blocked if it came with no compact policy or an unsatisfactory one. A first-party cookie with an unsatisfactory policy was downgraded to a session cookie.
fieldFixes.legalForce: None in itself. The browser had 'no technical means' to enforce the claims. A false policy might have been challenged as deceptive: Microsoft said it could ground a lawsuit, and Lorrie Cranor said the FTC or state attorneys general 'could go after' such sites. No regulator is known to have acted. Sites discovered that an invalid or even self-declared non-policy ('This is not a P3P policy!') still got their cookies accepted.
fieldFixes.fate: Widely gamed. In 2010, 11,176 of 33,139 sites had erroneous compact policies, and 98% of the invalid ones left cookies unblocked under IE's default setting. Google's and Facebook's non-policies drew wide attention in February 2012. The compact policy was retired with P3P in 2018, when the W3C said no current user agents were known to act on P3P policies.

issues: body says the header was 'Proposed by Christopher Soghoian and Sid Stamm'. That overstates their role and leaves out who wrote the specification the W3C used. Soghoian's own history says Stamm 'helped me to put together a prototype Firefox add-on' in July 2009, and credits earlier header suggestions (Mozilla's Mike Shaver, March 2009; a conversation with Dan Kaminsky). The W3C Note says: 'The DNT header field is based on the original Do Not Track submission by Jonathan Mayer (Stanford), Arvind Narayanan (Stanford), and Sid Stamm (Mozilla).'

Three dated claims in years and fate had no source on the record: 'prototype July 2009', 'Firefox 4, March 2011' and 'Microsoft stopped enabling it by default in 2015'. All three are true, and primary sources for them are added below.

Everything else checks out. The DNT value definitions ('1 This user prefers not to be tracked on this request.' / '0 This user prefers to allow tracking on this request.') and the Tk response header are in the W3C Note of 17 January 2019. The Note's status says there had 'not been sufficient deployment of these extensions' and 'The working group has therefore decided to conclude its work', which supports 'closed in January 2019 citing insufficient deployment'. The White House release (23 February 2012) has the FTC-enforcement sentence and 'agreed to comply when consumers choose to control online tracking'. Safari 12.1 was 'Released March 25, 2019' with DNT removed 'to prevent potential use as a fingerprinting variable'.

Minor, no change: 'One bit' simplifies the grammar, which is DNT-field-value = ( "0" / "1" ) *DNT-extension. The Note leaves room for extensions but defines none: 'Servers that do not implement DNT extensions SHOULD ignore anything beyond the first character'. So 'carries no purposes, conditions or terms' stands.

fieldFixes.body: Prototyped by Christopher Soghoian and Sid Stamm (2009). The header field was specified in a Do Not Track submission by Jonathan Mayer, Arvind Narayanan and Sid Stamm. It was shipped by Mozilla and other browser makers, and standardised by the W3C Tracking Protection Working Group (Tracking Preference Expression).
